name: Claude Architect Foundations (CCA-F) - Mock 3
source: Community-authored full-length practice exam for the Anthropic Claude Certified Architect Foundations (CCA-F) exam. 60 single-answer questions across 4 scenarios, each with an explanation. These are practice questions, not real exam items.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

Production logs show that 8% of refunds skip validate_refund_eligibility and call process_refund directly, resulting in compliance violations. The system prompt already states: "Always call validate_refund_eligibility before processing any refund." What change most effectively eliminates these violations?
options: Strengthen the system prompt: "Skipping eligibility validation is a critical compliance violation that must never occur."
Add few-shot examples demonstrating the correct validate-then-refund sequence across multiple scenarios
Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that blocks execution unless validate_refund_eligibility has returned a verified result for that order
Rename validate_refund_eligibility to mandatory_pre_refund_check to make the dependency obvious in the tool name
cards.a: C. Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that blocks execution unless validate_refund_eligibility has returned a verified result for that order
cards.explanation:
An 8% failure rate means a probabilistic mechanism is already losing. Financial compliance requires deterministic enforcement. A PreToolUse hook on process_refund places the check outside Claude's decision-making, the tool simply cannot run until the precondition is met.

Trap pattern: A and B are both probabilistic (Trap 6, more of what's already failing). D is Trap 2, a more descriptive name hints but cannot enforce. Firm language in a system prompt never reaches 0% failure.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A PostToolUse hook is added to process_refund. It checks the refund amount and sends an alert if it exceeds $500. Despite this, a $650 refund completes successfully without escalation. What is the root cause?
options: The hook is inspecting the tool result object rather than the tool input arguments, it should check the amount parameter before the call
The alert threshold should trigger a block, not just a notification, change the hook to reject the tool call
PostToolUse fires after the tool has already executed; the refund has already completed by the time the hook runs, so it cannot prevent anything
The hook should be attached to validate_refund_eligibility instead, where the amount is first confirmed
cards.a: C. PostToolUse fires after the tool has already executed; the refund has already completed by the time the hook runs, so it cannot prevent anything
cards.explanation:
PostToolUse fires after execution. By the time it runs, the money has already moved. To prevent a transaction, the enforcement must be PreToolUse, which fires before the tool runs. PostToolUse's job is normalising data on the way back to the model, not blocking operations.

Trap pattern: A describes a real design mistake but is not the root cause. D is Trap 9, switching timing (Pre to Post or vice versa) without recognising that only PreToolUse can block.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

get_customer has the description: "Gets customer data." After the system prompt was updated to include "review all customer records before processing any transaction," the agent began calling get_customer for order lookups that don't require customer data at all. Tool descriptions are unchanged. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The get_customer description is too vague; rewrite it with explicit use cases, example inputs, and boundaries
The system prompt phrase 'customer records' keyword-matches the get_customer tool name; rephrase the system prompt to avoid the accidental association
Add few-shot examples showing correct tool selection between get_customer and lookup_order
Merge get_customer and lookup_order into a single get_customer_with_order composite tool
cards.a: B. The system prompt phrase 'customer records' keyword-matches the get_customer tool name; rephrase the system prompt to avoid the accidental association
cards.explanation:
The stem provides two eliminating facts: descriptions are unchanged AND the problem started after the system prompt update. This means the update is the cause. The phrase 'customer records' in the system prompt accidentally keyword-matches the get_customer tool name.

Trap pattern: A, C, and D are all eliminated by Trap 4, the stem rules them out by stating descriptions are unchanged and identifying when the problem began. 'After X, Y started happening' means X is the cause.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

process_refund calls a payment API. When the API key expires, the tool returns {"success": true, "refunds": [], "status": "Authentication failed"}. The agent responds "No refunds found for this customer" and closes the case. What is the root cause?
options: Instruct the agent via system prompt to treat empty refund arrays as potential errors requiring additional verification steps
The tool cannot distinguish an authentication failure from a valid empty result; it should return isError: true with errorCategory: 'permission' on auth failure
The third-party payment API is returning a misleading success flag; this is a vendor problem requiring an API contract fix
A PostToolUse hook should parse the status field and convert 'Authentication failed' into a structured error signal
cards.a: B. The tool cannot distinguish an authentication failure from a valid empty result; it should return isError: true with errorCategory: 'permission' on auth failure
cards.explanation:
'Found nothing' is not the same as 'couldn't look.' The tool masks an access failure as a successful empty result. The fix is at the tool layer: return isError: true with the appropriate errorCategory. The agent is behaving correctly given the information it received.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 6, a prompt instruction cannot distinguish the two cases structurally. C is Trap 7, you control the tool layer and must handle upstream misbehaviour there. D is Trap 2, prose parsing in hooks is fragile; the tool design is the right fix.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

process_refund returns HTTP 503 on server overload (transient) and HTTP 404 when an order ID doesn't exist in the system (permanent). The agent retries both identically. After exhausting retries on 404s, the server recovers but the retry budget is spent. What structural change to the error response fixes this?
options: Include the raw HTTP status code in the error message text so the agent can read and branch on it
Return a structured errorCategory field ('transient' vs 'business') with an isRetryable boolean flag
Increase the retry limit from 3 to 10 to give transient errors more opportunities to succeed
Add a system prompt rule: 'Do not retry requests that return a 404 status code'
cards.a: B. Return a structured errorCategory field ('transient' vs 'business') with an isRetryable boolean flag
cards.explanation:
Structured error categories allow the agent to apply correct retry logic without parsing prose. A 503-overload is transient (retry as-is). A 404-missing-order is a permanent business error (never retry). The distinction must be in the response structure, not inferred from a status code embedded in text.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 7, more information but still requires fragile string parsing. C is Trap 6, more retries don't fix misclassification. D is Trap 6, a prompt instruction is probabilistic.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

Incoming documents are standard refund requests, chargeback disputes, or warranty claims, each with a different extraction schema implemented as a separate tool. Documents arrive in all three types mixed together. The agent must always produce structured output and never return plain text. The document type is determined by reading the document. Which tool_choice setting is correct?
options: {"type": "auto"} - Claude decides whether to call a tool based on document content
{"type": "any"} - Claude must call a tool but selects which schema fits the document
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_standard_refund"} - ensures consistent structured output regardless of type
Omit tool_choice; a system prompt instruction tells Claude to always call the appropriate extraction tool
cards.a: B. {"type": "any"} - Claude must call a tool but selects which schema fits the document
cards.explanation:
The document type is UNKNOWN until Claude reads it, Claude must choose the schema. 'any' guarantees a tool call while leaving schema selection to the model. This is the right setting whenever the choice is genuinely the model's to make.

Trap pattern: C welds every document to the standard-refund schema regardless of type, it produces structured output but always the wrong structure for chargebacks and warranty claims. A allows a prose response (no guarantee). D is probabilistic.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A customer disputes a 45-day-old charge of $4,200. The agent confirms the charge is legitimate and has explained the 30-day refund policy twice. The customer repeats their dissatisfaction but has not explicitly asked to speak with a manager. Company policy is silent on any accommodation outside the 30-day window. What most justifies escalation at this moment?
options: The customer's repeated frustration indicates a need for human empathy the agent cannot adequately provide
The $4,200 transaction value exceeds a threshold that warrants human review by default
Company policy is silent on out-of-window accommodations; a human must make that judgement call
The 45-day transaction age creates potential legal complexity outside the agent's area of expertise
cards.a: C. Company policy is silent on out-of-window accommodations; a human must make that judgement call
cards.explanation:
Escalate on authority, not on discomfort and not on size. The policy is silent on this case, the agent has no authority to decide. That policy gap is a valid escalation trigger. The customer hasn't explicitly requested a human, so that trigger isn't available; the gap in authority is.

Trap pattern: A is escalating on emotional discomfort (invalid trigger). B is escalating on transaction value or size (invalid trigger). D is Trap 7, speculated complexity is not a trigger. Only three triggers are valid: explicit human request, policy gap, genuine inability to progress.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

The escalate_to_human tool is called with {"customer_id": "C-7712", "issue": "Refund requested"}. The human agent must call the customer back for more information, forcing the customer to re-explain from scratch. Which fields were missing from the handoff?
options: The order ID, a summary of actions already taken, the root cause of the denial, and a recommended next action
The customer's full name, preferred contact method, and account tier
A verbatim transcript of the conversation so the human can review the full exchange
A confidence score indicating how certain the agent was about its refund decision
cards.a: A. The order ID, a summary of actions already taken, the root cause of the denial, and a recommended next action
cards.explanation:
The human agent cannot see the conversation transcript. The handoff must be fully self-contained: customer ID, order ID, issue summary, actions taken, root cause, recommended next action. Every missing field forces the customer to re-explain something the agent already established.

Trap pattern: B contains supplementary details but misses the operationally critical fields. C is wrong, 'humans don't get the transcript' is the entire reason the handoff format exists. D is Trap 3, confidence scores from models are unreliable and not a handoff requirement.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A Pydantic model validates refund extractions. All required fields pass validation. However, 4% of processed refunds fail downstream because refund_amount doesn't equal the sum of the individual line_items. Pydantic reports no validation errors on these cases. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add stricter per-field constraints to refund_amount: minimum value, maximum decimal places, and numeric type enforcement
Add a @model_validator that runs after Pydantic parsing and verifies refund_amount equals sum(line_items), producing a specific error message if they diverge
Make refund_amount an optional field to prevent the model from hallucinating values when amounts are unclear
Add few-shot examples in the extraction prompt showing correct refund calculations
cards.a: B. Add a @model_validator that runs after Pydantic parsing and verifies refund_amount equals sum(line_items), producing a specific error message if they diverge
cards.explanation:
Pydantic validates the shape and type of individual fields. It cannot express rules that span multiple fields, that requires a cross-field validator. The specific error message it produces ('stated total 500 but line items sum to 450') is the third ingredient of an effective retry.

Trap pattern: A tightens per-field constraints but cannot check relationships between fields. C makes the problem worse by hiding the field entirely. D is Trap 3, examples reduce the frequency but cannot perform arithmetic validation.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

Compliance requires that every refund is logged to an audit system before the transaction completes. This rule must hold 100% of the time, for every agent, in every session, with no exceptions. Currently it lives in the project .claude/CLAUDE.md. The rule is violated in 2% of sessions. What is the root cause and correct fix?
options: Move the rule from project-level to user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for stronger personal enforcement
Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that invokes the audit logging tool before allowing the refund to execute
Strengthen the CLAUDE.md instruction with more explicit language: 'CRITICAL: audit logging is MANDATORY before every refund'
Create a /log-then-refund skill that developers invoke to ensure the correct sequence
cards.a: B. Add a PreToolUse hook on process_refund that invokes the audit logging tool before allowing the refund to execute
cards.explanation:
'100% of the time, no exceptions' means deterministic enforcement. CLAUDE.md is probabilistic, Claude reads it as guidance and weighs it alongside everything else in context. Contradictions may resolve arbitrarily. Only hooks and settings.json enforce deterministically. PreToolUse on process_refund cannot be bypassed by Claude's reasoning.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 1 and makes things worse, user-level scope means team members never receive it. C is Trap 6, firmer language in a prompt moves the failure rate, never to zero. D is Trap 6, a skill is task-triggered and probabilistic.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A new compliance requirement states that a risk classification must be logged before any subagent is created by the coordinator. Which hook and attachment point implement this deterministically?
options: A SubagentStart hook that logs the classification when the subagent begins initialising
A PreToolUse hook on the Task tool that logs the risk classification before the subagent is spawned
A PostToolUse hook on the Task tool that records the classification after each subagent completes
A system prompt instruction to the coordinator: 'Always log risk classification before creating any subagent'
cards.a: B. A PreToolUse hook on the Task tool that logs the risk classification before the subagent is spawned
cards.explanation:
The Task tool is how coordinators spawn subagents. PreToolUse on Task fires before the subagent is created, the earliest available enforcement point. This is deterministic: Claude cannot bypass it.

Trap pattern: A is wrong, SubagentStart fires when the subagent initialises (after creation) and cannot block. C is wrong, PostToolUse fires after the subagent completes (too late for a 'before creation' requirement). D is Trap 6, probabilistic.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

Three refund-processing subagents handle different categories. When the warranty_refund subagent times out, it returns {"status": "unavailable"}. The coordinator marks the entire batch failed and discards results already completed by the other two subagents. What anti-pattern does this represent?
options: Silent suppression - the subagent is not distinguishing between a connection failure and a valid empty result
Workflow termination - aborting the entire pipeline on a single subagent failure and discarding completed work
Context degradation - the coordinator has lost track of which subagents completed successfully
Attention dilution - too many concurrent subagents are competing for coordinator attention
cards.a: B. Workflow termination - aborting the entire pipeline on a single subagent failure and discarding completed work
cards.explanation:
Workflow termination discards completed work when one specialist fails. The other two subagents finished successfully, their results are valuable and should be preserved. The correct pattern is for the coordinator to use partial results, log the timeout, and decide whether to retry only the failed specialist.

Trap pattern: A is a different anti-pattern (returning empty as success when access failed). The returned 'unavailable' here is at least honest about failure. C and D are different context problems entirely.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A CI pipeline runs daily: claude -p "Verify all refund policy rules in src/policy/ are documented in docs/compliance/". It consistently reports 100% compliance. Manual audits regularly find undocumented rules. What is the most likely cause?
options: The -p flag restricts Claude's file access in CI, preventing it from reading all relevant policy files
Without explicit validation criteria defining what 'documented' means, Claude performs a shallow check and reports a confident but inaccurate result
--output-format json should be added so the CI environment can properly parse and evaluate the findings
A second independent Claude instance should verify the first instance's findings before reporting
cards.a: B. Without explicit validation criteria defining what 'documented' means, Claude performs a shallow check and reports a confident but inaccurate result
cards.explanation:
'Verify that rules are documented' is a vague instruction with no defined criteria. Claude has no explicit definition of what constitutes documentation coverage, so it performs a shallow scan and reports confidently. A check that never fails isn't checking, the instruction is the problem.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 8, -p makes the session non-interactive, it does not restrict tool access. C is Trap 7, JSON format affects output structure, not analysis quality. D is Trap 5, a second instance reading the same vague prompt draws the same conclusion.

cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

Code review findings show developer trust eroding. A survey reveals: 'We've stopped reading findings, too many false positives in style and naming categories make everything look noisy.' High-precision categories (security, logic errors) are now being ignored along with the noise. What is the best approach to restore trust?
options: Temporarily disable high-false-positive categories (style, naming) and keep only high-precision categories while improving the disabled ones
Show a confidence score alongside each finding so developers can filter by confidence threshold
Add a second model pass to verify each finding before surfacing it to reduce false positives
Raise the severity threshold uniformly so only critical findings are reported across all categories
cards.a: A. Temporarily disable high-false-positive categories (style, naming) and keep only high-precision categories while improving the disabled ones
cards.explanation:
Trust is broken because developers have stopped reading entirely. Any solution that still requires reading (confidence scores, severity filters) fails the people who have already disengaged. Removing the noise source directly restores the signal. Cut coverage to restore credibility.

Trap pattern: B is Trap 7, confidence scores require reading; developers have already stopped. C is Trap 5, a second pass on low-precision prompts still has low precision. D is Trap 10, raising the threshold hides valid medium-severity findings.

cards.topic: Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
cards.q:
Scenario 1: Meridian Bank - Refund Processing Agent
Meridian Bank builds a customer refund agent with five tools: get_customer(customer_id), lookup_order(order_id), validate_refund_eligibility(order_id, customer_id), process_refund(order_id, amount), escalate_to_human(handoff_data). Policy requires eligibility verification before every refund. Refunds over $500 require manager approval.

A coordinator delegates to three subagents: chargeback_specialist, warranty_specialist, fraud_specialist. The coordinator was loaded with Meridian's complete policy documents at session start. The fraud_specialist's reports consistently contain no policy references despite the policies being directly relevant. What is the root cause?
options: The fraud_specialist subagent is not fine-tuned on Meridian Bank's specific policy content
The coordinator is not passing the relevant policy content into the fraud_specialist's task prompt; subagents do not inherit coordinator context
The subagents should run sequentially so the fraud_specialist can build on the other specialists' policy-referenced findings
Add a policy query tool to the fraud_specialist so it can retrieve policy content independently on demand
cards.a: B. The coordinator is not passing the relevant policy content into the fraud_specialist's task prompt; subagents do not inherit coordinator context
cards.explanation:
Subagent isolation. The fraud_specialist starts blank, it sees only what the coordinator writes into its task prompt. Policy documents loaded into the coordinator's context are not shared automatically. The coordinator must explicitly inject the relevant policy sections into each task prompt it writes.

Trap pattern: A is false, subagents use the same model. C is wrong, sequencing doesn't transfer coordinator context to subagents. D is Trap 5, it works but adds a tool call for information the coordinator already holds and could inject directly.

cards.topic: Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

DevStream's team creates a /security-audit skill. Three requirements: (1) available to every developer on the project, (2) cannot modify any files, (3) produces extensive output that must not pollute the main conversation. Which configuration is correct?
options: ~/.claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with allowed-tools: ["Read","Grep","Glob"] and context: fork
.claude/commands/security-audit.md with allowed-tools: ["Read","Grep","Glob"]
.claude/CLAUDE.md with a security scanning procedure written as an always-loaded instruction
.claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with allowed-tools: ["Read","Grep","Glob"] and context: fork
cards.a: D. .claude/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md with allowed-tools: ["Read","Grep","Glob"] and context: fork
cards.explanation:
Three requirements, three mechanisms. .claude/skills/ (not ~/.claude/) puts the file in the repo, shared on clone. allowed-tools: Read/Grep/Glob makes it read-only. context: fork isolates noisy output to a sub-session, keeping the main conversation clean.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 1, identical to D except for the ~/ prefix, which makes it personal, not shared. B is Trap 10, right folder structure, no context: fork (meets two of three requirements). C uses CLAUDE.md for a task-specific procedure, wrong mechanism.

cards.topic: Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A developer suspects their Claude Code session is not loading the project's CLAUDE.md conventions correctly, edits are being made with inconsistent standards. What is the fastest way to confirm which CLAUDE.md files the current session has actually loaded?
options: Ask Claude to list the conventions it is currently following
Run /compact to reset the session state and force a configuration reload
Delete ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to eliminate user-level configuration as a variable
Run /memory
cards.a: D. Run /memory
cards.explanation:
/memory is the diagnostic command. It shows which instruction files this session actually loaded. Asking Claude what conventions it follows produces plausible-sounding testimony, Claude can paraphrase conventions from training or partial context and sound completely confident, which proves nothing about what actually loaded.

Trap pattern: A is testimony vs evidence, the exam uses the word 'actually' as a tell. B is Trap 8, /compact summarises context, it doesn't reload configuration. C is Trap 5, destructive and not diagnostic; also makes the problem worse.

cards.topic: Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

DevStream has TypeScript test files (*.test.ts) scattered across 50+ directories. All test files should follow the same import ordering and assertion conventions. Where should these conventions live?
options: In the root CLAUDE.md, always loaded, applies to everything in the project
In a directory-level CLAUDE.md placed in each directory that contains tests
In .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/*.test.ts"] in the frontmatter
In a /testing skill that developers invoke when they begin working on tests
cards.a: C. In .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/*.test.ts"] in the frontmatter
cards.explanation:
'One file type, scattered across many directories' is the exact use case for path-scoped rules. .claude/rules/ with a paths: glob loads only when a matching file is touched, Terraform rules stay out of context during React work, test rules load only during test edits.

Trap pattern: A loads always, wasting tokens on every session regardless of whether tests are being touched. B requires creating 50+ separate files (not maintainable). D makes the convention task-triggered, developers must remember to invoke it.

cards.topic: Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A CI pipeline runs: claude -p "Verify API contracts haven't changed" --output-format json. A senior engineer tells a junior that the -p flag restricts Claude's file access in CI as a security measure. Is this correct?
options: Yes, -p enables a restricted security sandbox that limits file and tool access in non-interactive mode
No, -p makes the session non-interactive (print result and exit) but does not restrict tools or file access at all
Partially, -p restricts interactive tools like Bash but leaves read-only tools like Read and Grep available
Partially, -p is unrelated to file access; use --permission-mode to control actual restrictions
cards.a: B. No, -p makes the session non-interactive (print result and exit) but does not restrict tools or file access at all
cards.explanation:
-p (--print) changes how the session starts and ends: it takes the instruction, does the work, prints to stdout, and exits without waiting for user input. Claude Code retains full access to all configured tools. To restrict tool access, use --allowedTools or --disallowedTools explicitly.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 8, this restriction does not exist. C is Trap 8, same misconception, partially stated. D has a true fact about --permission-mode but incorrectly implies -p is unrelated to the question's premise.

cards.topic: Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A developer uses plan mode to investigate a complex bug affecting five services. After 20 minutes, they identify the fix: a single configuration value in one file. What is the correct next step?
options: Complete the entire session in plan mode to maintain investigation consistency
Start a new session in direct execution mode to apply the identified fix
Switch to direct execution mode within the current session and apply the fix
Stay in plan mode, fully document the fix, and hand off to a colleague to apply in a separate session
cards.a: C. Switch to direct execution mode within the current session and apply the fix
cards.explanation:
Plan mode is for ambiguity, not difficulty. Once the change is scoped to a single known fix, planning adds nothing. Switch to direct execution in the same session, starting a new session discards the investigation context that produced the fix.

Trap pattern: A, 'consistency' is a fake virtue. B loses the 20 minutes of investigation that identified the fix. D is Trap 5, unnecessary overhead; the developer has all the context they need.

Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A coordinator processes requests and delegates research to a research_subagent. The coordinator holds a comprehensive API documentation database at session start. The research_subagent's responses consistently miss API-specific constraints that were covered in the coordinator's context. What is the root cause?
options: The research_subagent needs to be connected to the same MCP server as the coordinator to access the documentation
The coordinator is not injecting the relevant API documentation into the research_subagent's task prompt; subagents do not automatically inherit coordinator context
The coordinator should handle all research tasks itself rather than delegating, since context cannot be transferred between agents
Run the research_subagent after the coordinator's analysis phase so it can build on prior work
cards.a: B. The coordinator is not injecting the relevant API documentation into the research_subagent's task prompt; subagents do not automatically inherit coordinator context
cards.explanation:
Subagent isolation. The research_subagent's entire world is the task prompt the coordinator writes. Documentation held in the coordinator's context is not inherited. The coordinator must explicitly copy the relevant sections into the task string it passes.

Trap pattern: A adds complexity for information the coordinator already holds. C defeats the purpose of delegation. D, sequencing doesn't transfer context; the subagent still starts blank regardless of when it runs.

A developer wants a personal /refactor-imports skill applying their own formatting preferences. This skill should not affect any other developer on the team. Where should the skill file be placed?
options: .claude/skills/refactor-imports/SKILL.md
~/.claude/skills/refactor-imports/SKILL.md
.claude/commands/refactor-imports.md
In the root CLAUDE.md under a personal preferences section
cards.a: B. ~/.claude/skills/refactor-imports/SKILL.md
cards.explanation:
Personal skill goes to ~/.claude/ (home folder, not committed to git, not shared). Team skill goes to .claude/ (repo, shared on clone). The tilde is the entire answer.

Trap pattern: A puts the skill in the repo, it is shared with every developer on clone (Trap 1). C is also in .claude/ and therefore shared. D is Trap 6, CLAUDE.md is loaded for everyone.

Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

DevStream wants to connect to: (1) a shared GitHub Enterprise instance for all 12 developers, (2) a patent search API for all developers, (3) an experimental personal data warehouse one developer is testing alone. Which MCP configuration is correct?
options: All three servers in .mcp.json, project-level config covers all team resources
GitHub Enterprise and patent API in .mcp.json; personal data warehouse in ~/.claude.json
GitHub Enterprise in ~/.claude/mcp.json; patent API and data warehouse in .mcp.json
All three servers in ~/.claude.json, MCP configuration should always be personal to avoid conflicts
cards.a: B. GitHub Enterprise and patent API in .mcp.json; personal data warehouse in ~/.claude.json
cards.explanation:
.mcp.json (project root) is shared with the team on clone. ~/.claude.json (home folder) is personal to the machine and not shared. Team-wide servers go in the project file; experimental personal servers go in the personal file.

Trap pattern: A shares the experimental server with the whole team. C uses the path ~/.claude/mcp.json which does not exist, the personal file is ~/.claude.json (a file, not a folder). D puts team-wide servers in personal config.

cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

DevStream's code review agent generates PR feedback. Analysis shows non-obvious issues are only caught in human review. When the generator's reasoning is examined, it shows Claude explicitly considered and dismissed these exact cases during code generation. What change most effectively addresses this?
options: Include the full test suite and documentation in the review agent's context so it has more information
Add few-shot examples of the non-obvious issue types that are currently being missed
Run a second review pass using the same agent instance with a higher temperature setting
Run an independent Claude instance for review without access to the generator's reasoning or prior decisions
cards.a: D. Run an independent Claude instance for review without access to the generator's reasoning or prior decisions
cards.explanation:
The stem makes the diagnosis explicit: 'Claude already considered and dismissed these cases.' More information is not the gap, independence is. A second instance that never saw the generation reasoning has no prior commitment to defend. It will challenge; the original instance will confirm.

Trap pattern: A and B are Trap 6, the stem eliminates them by stating Claude already considered these cases. C uses the same instance; it retains its original reasoning regardless of temperature.

cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A developer asks Claude to address three issues simultaneously: (1) fix a null pointer in the auth module, (2) update the test suite for that module, (3) update the API response schema that tests in issue 2 must conform to. What is the correct sequencing?
options: Address all three in a single message for maximum efficiency
Fix issues 1 and 2 first (they are directly related), then address 3
Fix issue 3 first (the schema change defines what tests in issue 2 must look like), then 1 and 2
Fix issue 1 first (the original bug), then 2, then 3 in logical dependency order
cards.a: C. Fix issue 3 first (the schema change defines what tests in issue 2 must look like), then 1 and 2
cards.explanation:
Three-part sequencing rule: resolve dependencies first, batch what interacts, sequence what's independent. Issue 3 changes the output shape that issue 2 must conform to. Fixing tests before the schema change means rewriting them immediately after. Fix 3 first, then 1 and 2.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 10, the three issues interfere with each other. B gets the dependency order backwards, tests written before the schema change immediately become stale. D is also the wrong order for the same reason.

cards.q:
Scenario 2: DevStream Platform - Developer Tooling
DevStream's 12-engineer team shares a monorepo. They use Claude Code for coding assistance and need consistent conventions, shared skills, CI integration, and personal developer customisations, all without stepping on each other.

A synthesis subagent calls back to the coordinator for every fact verification, even simple routine lookups. Analysis: 82% of verifications match a clear, stable pattern; 18% require coordinator judgment. Each round-trip adds 400ms. What is the best architectural fix?
options: Build a composite verify_and_synthesise tool that handles both routine and complex verifications in a single call
Give the synthesis subagent a scoped verify_fact tool for routine lookups (82%); route complex cases (18%) through the coordinator as before
Increase the coordinator's context window to handle more concurrent verification tasks efficiently
Spawn multiple synthesis subagents in parallel to amortise the round-trip overhead
cards.a: B. Give the synthesis subagent a scoped verify_fact tool for routine lookups (82%); route complex cases (18%) through the coordinator as before
cards.explanation:
An explicit 82/18 split signals: handle the common case locally with a scoped tool, escalate the exception. This is the tool distribution pattern. Adding the scoped tool eliminates 82% of round-trips without requiring coordinator judgment for them.

Trap pattern: A is Trap 5, a single tool can't selectively apply coordinator judgment. C is Trap 6, context window doesn't fix architecture. D is Trap 5, parallelism reduces wall-clock time for the 18% but doesn't eliminate the per-call overhead.
